title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the abdominal aorta that carries a risk of progressive enlargement and rupture, with the risk increasing with increasing diameter. Many aneurysms remain asymptomatic until expansion produces abdominal, back, or flank pain or until acute rupture causes hemodynamic instability. Ultrasonography supports timely detection and surveillance by providing rapid, noninvasive assessment of intraluminal diameter and characterization of intraluminal findings, such as thrombus or an intimal flap suggestive of dissection. Accurate technique emphasizes imaging in short- and long-axis views, identification of the maximal diameter, and leading-edge-to-leading-edge measurement to avoid under- or overestimation. Postendovascular aneurysm repair evaluation focuses on graft integrity and endoleak detection, often supplemented by Doppler methods when clinically appropriate.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Course participation builds competency in point-of-care ultrasonography workflows for aortic and related vascular assessments, including patient preparation, image optimization, standardized sweeps, and reproducible measurement techniques. Skill development includes recognizing high-risk ultrasonography findings (eg, aneurysm morphology, intraluminal thrombus, intimal flap, graft-related abnormalities) and appropriately documenting them to support clinical decision-making. Emphasis on Doppler fundamentals reinforces angle optimization and interpretation limits within variable clinical contexts. Collaboration with an interprofessional team consisting of a clinician, sonographer, nurse, and radiologist enhances outcomes through shared situational awareness, efficient room and equipment readiness, rapid escalation when images are inadequate, and coordinated selection of alternative diagnostic modalities when needed. Clear communication of findings and urgency across disciplines reduces delays, supports accurate diagnosis, and improves subsequent treatment planning.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Introduction
content: Several pathological conditions impact the abdominal vasculature, including aneurysms, dissections, atherosclerotic disease, and flow-limiting states. Abdominal aortic aneurysms are a potentially life-threatening conditions that affect at least 2% of adults older than age 50 years. [1] Ultrasonography is the ideal diagnostic modality for detecting aortic aneurysms due to its high sensitivity and specificity. [2] [3] [4] [5] However, ultrasonography's role is more limited in assessing other pathologies, such as aneurysmal rupture, aortic dissection, abdominal aortic stenosis, major branch pathology, and inferior vena cava pathology. Notably, there is no universal protocol for abdominal vascular imaging. The proposed protocol is a general guideline for evaluating the aorta, inferior vena cava, mesenteric arteries, and iliac arteries.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The abdominal aorta is the primary vessel that delivers oxygenated blood to the lower extremities and abdominal organs. The aorta begins just beneath the diaphragm and terminates at the bifurcation of the common iliac arteries. [6] The inferior vena cava is the primary vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from its tributaries within the abdomen, pelvis, and lower extremities to the heart. The inferior vena cava courses parallel and to the right of the aorta. The course begins at the confluence of the iliac veins and terminates at the right atrium.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Indications
content: The following are indications for abdominal point-of-care ultrasonography: Screening for abdominal aortic aneurysms Suspected iliac aneurysms Hypotension and suspected aortic pathology Absent pulses in the distal extremities Suspected mesenteric ischemia

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Contraindications
content: There are no absolute contraindications to performing this procedure.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Equipment -- Transducer Selection and Orientation
content: Transducers operating at 1.0 to 5.0 MHz provide adequate images for the typical adult patient. The frequency should be adjusted based on the patient's body habitus.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Personnel
content: This procedure can be performed by registered diagnostic medical sonographers or clinicians trained in ultrasonography.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Preparation
content: The patient should be fasting, typically for 4 to 6 hours, before imaging. Ideally, the patient should be supine during the examination. If the sonographer cannot obtain adequate images, the patient can be repositioned to a right or left lateral decubitus position. The examination should be performed in a darkened room.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Image Acquisition
content: The depth should be adjusted to visualize the vertebrae sonographically posterior to the aorta. In the short axis, a sweep of the entire length of the abdominal aorta spans from the diaphragm to the bifurcation of the common iliac vessels (see Image. Sagittal View of the Abdominal Aorta). The widest portion of the aorta should be identified and measured from the anterior leading edge to the posterior leading edge of the vessel. In the long axis, a sweep of the entire length of the abdominal aorta spans from the diaphragm to the bifurcation of the common iliac vessels. The widest portion of the aorta should be identified in the long axis and measured from the anterior leading edge to the posterior leading edge of the vessel.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Image Acquisition
content: Whenever an aneurysm is identified, its anatomic relationship to the renal arteries (eg, infrarenal or suprarenal), distance from the renal arteries, and the diameter should be documented. The right and left common iliac arteries should be visualized, and their greatest anterior-posterior diameter should be measured in the short and long axis from leading edge to leading edge. Any pathological findings identified by the sonographer, such as thrombi or flaps, should be documented. If an endograft is present, its proximal and distal attachment points should be noted. The sonographer should also apply color and spectral Doppler to assess flow within the graft lumen and the aneurysmal sac.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Additional Images of the Mesenteric Arteries
content: The sonographer can attempt to obtain spectral Doppler tracings of the mesenteric arteries. A Doppler angle of 60° or less should be used to maximize the accuracy of the Doppler velocities. [7] Peak systolic velocities of the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery should be measured.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Additional Images of the Inferior Vena Cava
content: The sonographer should identify the inferior vena cava in the short and long axes. In the long axis, the anteroposterior diameter should be measured 2 to 3 cm caudal from the vessel's confluence at the right atrium. The diameter should be measured during both inspiration and expiration.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Image Optimization and Accuracy
content: Bowel gas can often preclude the sonographer from obtaining adequate images. The sonographer can apply steady pressure to the abdomen to attempt to displace bowel gas. [8] Another method is to have the patient lie in a lateral decubitus position. Lastly, if images of the anterior abdominal wall are inadequate, the sonographer can attempt to visualize the aorta in coronal view between the anterior axillary and midaxillary lines.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment -- Image Optimization and Accuracy
content: Visualizing the aorta in both long and short axes helps ensure that pathological findings are not missed and increases the likelihood of accurate measurements. Measuring in the long axis may underestimate the vessel's diameter if the sonographer inadvertently measures lateral to the vessel's true midline, a phenomenon known as the cylinder tangent effect. [8] Conversely, measuring in the short plane risks overestimating the aortic diameter if the measurement is taken at an oblique angle. [9] Caution should be exercised to avoid these errors, and using measurements in both axes improves accuracy. If it is not possible to store video clips of sonographic images, still images of the abdominal aorta should be obtained in 2 planes at the levels of the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery, and proximal to the iliac bifurcation.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: There are no complications associated with this procedure.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Abdominal aortic aneurysm
content: Ultrasonography is highly sensitive and specific for detecting abdominal aortic aneurysms. [4] However, accepted normal values of the abdominal aortic diameter vary. The American College of Radiology recommends that an abdominal aortic diameter of 3 cm or greater should be considered aneurysmal. [10] The reference adult abdominal aortic diameter is approximately 2 cm, so a 3 cm result is considered abnormal. A vessel is considered aneurysmal once its diameter is 1.5 times larger than that of its contiguous aortic segment of normal diameter. [10] Diameters between 2 and 3 cm are classified as ectatic because their dilatation is less than 1.5 times the normal diameter. [10]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Abdominal aortic aneurysm
content: The annual risk of rupture of abdominal aortic aneurysms rises exponentially with increasing diameter. Aneurysms are commonly classified as either fusiform (involving a limited portion of the diameter of the vessel) or saccular (involving a limited portion of the diameter). This distinction is helpful because the differential diagnosis varies by aneurysm type.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Intraluminal pathology
content: The abdominal aorta lumen is anechoic on ultrasonography; any other intraluminal appearance is likely pathological. Hypoechoic structures adjacent to the aortic wall are likely intraluminal thrombi. These thrombi may reduce the apparent size of the aortic lumen; therefore, the diameter should be measured from the leading edge to the leading edge (see Image. Aortic Aneurysm and Thrombus). Furthermore, case reports have documented instances in which point-of-care ultrasonography identified complete aortic occlusion. [11]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Intraluminal pathology
content: A linear echogenic structure within the lumen of the aorta, called an intimal flap, that separates the aorta into 2 distinct lumens, is thought to be highly specific for aortic dissection. [12] Given the high morbidity and mortality associated with aortic dissections, the sonographer must be able to recognize this essential clinical finding. The aorta becomes increasingly tortuous with age. Occasionally, the sidewall of a tortuous aorta can appear similar to an intraluminal clot. This potential pitfall supports imaging the aorta in 2 orthogonal planes, as pathology is typically visible in both planes.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Postendovascular graft assessment
content: Sonographers should be familiar with the normal appearance of endovascular grafts, given the increasing prevalence of this procedure. The sonographer should assess for fluid collections at the graft site and for endoleak by applying color and spectral Doppler to evaluate for flow within the aneurysm sac outside the graft. [13]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- The major types of endoleaks:
content: Type I: Occurs at the distal or proximal attachment sites Type II: Usually secondary to retrograde flow from aortic branch vessels into the sac Type III: Often results from graft structural failure Type IV: Occurs due to the porosity of the stent Type V: Occurs when the aneurysm expands [14]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance
content: Results from a 2017 Cochrane review reported that the sensitivity and specificity of color Doppler ultrasonography range from 82% to 91% and 93% to 96%, respectively. [15] Results from a 2022 cohort study published in Diagnostics comparing contrast-enhanced ultrasonography with Duplex ultrasonography for follow-up after endovascular aneurysm repair found that contrast-enhanced ultrasonography achieved higher sensitivity than Doppler ultrasonography (100% sensitivity vs 75%; P < .0001); for detecting type II endoleaks, contrast-enhanced ultrasonography demonstrated markedly higher sensitivity (93.2% vs 59.4%) with equivalent specificity (99.3%). [16]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Pathological Findings of the Iliac Arteries
content: Similar to findings of the abdominal aorta, the iliac arteries can be aneurysmal, contain thrombi, or have intraluminal flaps. The appearance of these findings is similar to that described for the aorta. The common iliac arteries are considered aneurysmal when the diameter exceeds 1.5 cm. [17]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Pathological Findings of the Mesenteric Arteries
content: Variables such as bowel gas, body habitus, and the timing of the patient’s most recent meal can complicate the interpretation of Doppler tracings. Various reference ranges for peak systolic velocities have been described for the mesenteric arteries. [18] [19] [20] [21] There is little consensus regarding the threshold at which peak systolic velocities correlate with a clinically significant degree of stenosis. [22] Findings should therefore be considered in conjunction with institutional thresholds and the patient’s clinical condition.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance -- Pathological Findings of the Inferior Vena Cava
content: On ultrasonography, the inferior vena cava should be anechoic within its lumen. Hypoechogenicity within the lumen, such as in the setting of thrombi or an inferior vena cava filter, is an example of intraluminal findings that should be documented. The anteroposterior diameter of the inferior vena cava is often used to predict fluid responsiveness in critically ill individuals. Although the inferior vena cava diameter and collapsibility can estimate central venous pressure, these measurements are inconsistent in predicting a patient’s intravascular volume status or fluid responsiveness. [23] [24] [25] [26]

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Interprofessional education and collaboration can improve the effectiveness of point-of-care ultrasonography evaluations. With a general understanding of the procedures involved and the equipment required to conduct the studies, healthcare professionals can anticipate one another's needs. For example, an emergency department technician or nurse who can anticipate the necessary materials (eg, gel, patient gown, transducers) and room conditions (eg, lighting, patient positioning, or bed height) significantly enhances patient care by reducing the time the sonographer or clinician spends preparing for procedures. Likewise, clinicians or sonographers should understand the relative importance of the sonogram within the patient's overall evaluation so that more urgent tasks or studies are not delayed.

title: Sonography Abdominal Vascular Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: If the sonographer has difficulty obtaining adequate images, an immediate discussion with the interprofessional care team and the radiologist is required to consider alternative diagnostic modalities. Nurses should also be included in any discussion of the procedure and the examination's findings. This type of interprofessional healthcare team communication can help ensure more accurate diagnosis and subsequent treatment, and improve patient outcomes.
